messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Waiter/Waitress
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 58

**Patient Vignette: “Mei”**

Mei is a 48-year-old woman of Southeast Asian descent who works as a waitress at a busy family-style restaurant in the suburbs. She is divorced and lives alone in a small apartment. She came to therapy at the urging of her manager, who noticed she had become “jumpy” and tearful at work, especially when male customers lingered at her tables.

The trauma began about fourteen months ago. A man started coming to the restaurant where Mei works. At first, he seemed like a regular—polite, quiet, tipped well. He always asked to sit in her section. She remembers feeling a small, private pleasure at the attention; she had been lonely since her divorce. Over several weeks, his visits increased. He began to linger after his meal, waiting for her to finish her shift. He would wait in the parking lot, leaning against his car, watching. She told him once, politely, that she was not interested. He smiled and said, “I’m not asking.”

The stalking escalated. He began leaving small notes on her car windshield. “You look tired today.” “I like your hair up.” The notes were never threatening in their content, but the fact that he had watched her, noticed her, made her stomach clench. She changed her route home. He found her new route. He began calling the restaurant, asking when she was working next. Her coworkers started to notice. The manager told her to “just ignore him,” that he was “probably harmless.” Mei felt shame, as if she had somehow invited this.

The final incident happened on a rainy night in November. She finished her shift at 10:30 p.m. As she walked to her car, she saw his silhouette in the driver’s seat of his car, parked three spaces away. He did not get out. He simply watched her unlock her door, get in, and drive away. For the first time, she felt real terror—not just discomfort, but a primal certainty that he could hurt her. She called the police the next day. They took a report, but without a direct threat, little was done. He stopped coming to the restaurant after that, but she never felt safe again.

Now, in the present, Mei’s life has contracted. She no longer parks in the restaurant lot; she takes the bus, even though it adds forty minutes to her commute. She scans every male customer’s face as they enter, her shoulders rising to her ears. When a man sits alone in her section, she feels a cold sweat bloom on her lower back. She has started to forget drink orders, to mix up tables. Her manager, a kind woman, has written her up twice for “poor customer service.” Mei does not tell her the truth—that she is terrified of making eye contact, of being noticed again.

At home, she checks her locks three times before bed. She sleeps with the lights on. She has stopped going to the grocery store after dark. She avoids the mailbox if she sees a car idling nearby. She replays the months of stalking in her head, searching for what she could have done differently. “I should have been rude,” she tells herself. “I should have screamed.” The shame is a physical weight in her chest.

She has not dated since the divorce. She tells herself she is not interested, but the truth is she cannot imagine trusting a man again. She feels watched, even when she is alone. On the bus, she sits with her back to the wall. In her apartment, she keeps the curtains drawn.

Mei is tired. She is tired of being afraid, tired of the vigilance, tired of the way her body remembers the threat even when her mind tells her he is gone. She came to therapy because she wants to feel like herself again—the woman who used to laugh with customers, who walked home without looking over her shoulder. She does not know if that woman still exists.
